docs.title: From Prototype to Production
docs.text:
Plenty of courses teach you to beat a benchmark in a notebook, and plenty more teach you to pitch a demo, hackathon style. But a demo has no real customer, no real deployment, and no real stakes: nobody depends on it, nothing breaks when it fails, and nobody needs to maintain it. This CMU course is about the hard part that comes next: turning that prototype into a production-grade AI-powered software system that delivers value to actual customers, that you deploy in the real world, and that keeps running, keeps getting updated, and adapts to changing conditions without going up in flames through security holes, safety incidents, or silent quality collapse.

You will learn AI engineering end to end, working across traditional machine learning, large language models, and, increasingly, AI agents that take actions in the real world: how to build the system around the model, ship it, know whether it actually works, anticipate the ways it will fail, and keep it operating and improving under real load. Along the way, we examine how familiar software engineering practices must adapt when system behavior is probabilistic, depends on data, and evolves over time. Because models make mistakes, and agents act on those mistakes, managing risk runs through the entire course, alongside MLOps and responsible AI (safety, security, explainability, fairness). The emphasis is on engineering complete systems that people can depend on.

This course is adapted from Machine Learning in Production (17-445/17-645/17-745) for an audience that is already familiar with software engineering practices. This Spring 2027 offering is designed for students with a software engineering background (e.g., 17-313 or equivalent experience with testing, requirements, architecture, process, and teamwork), some data science and GenAI experience (e.g., has taken a machine learning course, has used sklearn and LLMs), and basic programming skills (e.g., Python programming with libraries, navigating a Unix shell). Rather than introducing software engineering fundamentals, the course builds on them and focuses on what changes when systems depend on learned models, data, and agents.

docs.title: Official Course Description
docs.text: This course prepares software engineers to build and operate production-grade systems powered by machine learning. Assuming prior knowledge of software engineering and basic machine learning, it examines how established engineering practices must adapt to probabilistic, data-dependent, and continuously evolving behavior. Students study the full application lifecycle for systems integrating ML models, large language models, and AI agents. Topics include MLOps practices such as pipeline automation, versioning, reproducibility, deployment, monitoring, and drift detection; harness engineering for increasingly autonomous systems, including orchestration, evaluation, guardrails, permissions, and human oversight; and system-level qualities such as safety, security, privacy, fairness, and explainability.

docs.title: Who This Course Is For
docs.text:
This course is for students who want to build and operate AI-powered software systems that people can depend on. We assume familiarity with core software engineering practices from 17-313 or equivalent experience or coursework, along with basic machine learning, including training and evaluating a model. Building on that foundation, we explore what it takes to deploy a model, determine whether it works well enough, manage its failures, and operate and improve the system as data and the world change.

The course is particularly suited to software engineers who want to build production ML systems and AI agents, including students interested in roles such as AI Engineer, ML Engineer, MLOps Engineer, or Forward Deployed Engineer. Students will learn how to adapt familiar engineering practices to systems whose behavior depends on learned models, data, and probabilistic outputs. Through hands-on work, they will gain experience with ML pipelines, deployment, monitoring, behavioral testing, and production infrastructure.

The course also introduces harness engineering for AI agents: the tools, context, execution controls, and evaluation mechanisms that support reliable operation. Students will apply these ideas to an operations agent that uses production monitoring tools to help investigate incidents, with attention to permissions, security, failure recovery, and human oversight.

docs.title: What We Cover
docs.text:
Building on prior experience or coursework in software engineering and machine learning, we focus on the engineering challenges of building, deploying, and operating production ML systems, with additional emphasis on AI agents and harness engineering.

We cover topics such as:

  • How do we design for wrong predictions a model may make? How do we anticipate mistakes, assess risks, and assure safety despite possible errors? How do we design the user interface and the entire system to mitigate the consequences of mistakes? Where should we introduce human oversight?
  • How do we build and operate reliable AI agents? How does harness engineering support agents through context management, tool interfaces, and execution control? How do we connect agents to tools and APIs through protocols such as MCP? How do we use tracing, permissions, approval boundaries, and failure recovery to support reliable operation? How do we evaluate and secure an operations agent that helps diagnose production incidents?
  • How do we reliably deploy, monitor, and update models in production? How do MLOps tools support pipeline automation and continuous delivery? How do we manage versioning, provenance, and reproducibility across code, data, and models? How do we monitor system behavior, detect data quality issues and concept drift, and support safe updates and rollback?
  • How do we scale production ML systems? How do we handle growing volumes of training data, telemetry, and prediction requests? How do we use stream processing and production infrastructure to support reliable data ingestion and model serving? How do we balance latency, throughput, resource use, and operating cost?
  • How do we test and evaluate production ML systems and agents? How do we assess model quality beyond aggregate accuracy through data slicing and behavioral testing? How do we test data transformations, model integration, and entire ML pipelines? How do we incorporate these checks into continuous integration? For agents, how do we evaluate tool use, execution trajectories, and responses to tool failures and injected incidents?
  • Which qualities matter beyond prediction accuracy? How do we identify and measure application-specific requirements for latency, cost, scalability, explainability, fairness, and safety? How do we make model predictions and agent actions understandable? How do we recognize feedback loops, address accountability, and resolve conflicts among quality requirements?

Production-ready tools. You will gain familiarity with production-quality infrastructure tools. These are likely to include stream processing with Apache Kafka, test automation with GitHub Actions, monitoring and experiment tracking with tools such as Prometheus, Grafana, DVC, and Weights & Biases, and deployment with Docker, Kubernetes, and various MLOps tools. The exact set is still being finalized. Familiarity with these tools has helped many past Machine Learning in Production students in technical interviews.

Examples and case studies. We explore real products with commercial potential, going beyond benchmark tasks. For example, instead of object detection in the abstract, we look at how to use it in delivery robots or for image search on a photo-sharing site. Some of these products may be less flashy but have real commercial potential today, such as customer support agents, insurance fraud investigation, content recommendation, meeting minutes generated from recordings, and disease diagnosis.

An extended team project. Your team will build, deploy, evaluate, and maintain a robust and scalable movie recommendation service under realistic production conditions, serving one million active users. This is not a toy: your system runs live for several weeks and is graded on how it holds up under real load and changing conditions, as well as on the quality of your engineering decisions and evaluation. You will feel firsthand what breaks when a model meets production, and how to fix it.

docs.title: Practical Learning Experience
docs.text:
Through individual assignments, practical labs, case studies, and an extended team project, students will gain experience with:

  • Building and evaluating the complete software system around a model.
  • Using production infrastructure for automated testing, deployment, monitoring, and experiment tracking.
  • Making pipelines and experiments reproducible.
  • Identifying failures and responding to changing data and operating conditions.
  • Designing safeguards, permissions, and human oversight for increasingly autonomous systems.
  • Reasoning about tradeoffs among quality, latency, operating cost, scalability, safety, security, privacy, fairness, and explainability.

Examples and case studies emphasize real applications with practical and commercial value, going beyond isolated benchmark tasks.

Note

Specific tools and detailed course content are still being planned.

docs.title: Course Details
docs.text:
• Course number: 17-444
  • Course title: Production Machine Learning Systems for Software Engineers
  • Units: 9
  • Schedule: Two sessions per week, usually lectures; recitations every other week.
  • Expected background: Prior knowledge of software engineering and basic machine learning.
  • Software engineering preparation: 17-313, or significant software engineering experience subject to instructor approval.
  • Counts toward: CS elective.
  • Additional credit: Software Engineering Concentration credit to be confirmed.
  • Final exam: None.

docs.title: Proposed Assessment Structure
docs.text:
Proposed

The assessment structure below is proposed and may change before the semester begins.

Component Weight Description Individual assignments 35% Implementation, evaluation, and written analysis applying course concepts. Team project 30% Building, deploying, evaluating, and maintaining an AI-powered service through staged milestones. Midterms 20% Applying course concepts and reasoning through engineering decisions and tradeoffs. Labs 10% Practical exercises with production AI engineering tools and workflows. Participation 5% Contributions to discussions and in-class activities. Total 100% No final exam.

docs.title: Syllabus
docs.text:
Draft

This syllabus is a draft for Spring 2027 and may change before the semester begins.

docs.title: Course Syllabus and Policies
docs.text: The course is currently planned to be entirely in person for lectures, labs, and recitations. Most office hours will be in person, but some may be held over Zoom as well. The course uses Gradescope for assignment submission and grading; slides and handouts are posted here on the course website; GitHub is used to coordinate team work. We also use Slack for communication and team work: check your email during the first week of classes for the Slack sign up link.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This class has a prerequisite of 17-313 Foundations of Software Engineering or equivalent software engineering experience (for example, a summer course or an internship). We also assume basic machine learning knowledge, including training and evaluating a model. If you have not taken 17-313 but think you have similar experience, please get in touch with the instructor to obtain a waiver.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
The primary form of communication within this course is through Slack. We will make announcements through a dedicated channel in Slack, and also provide channels for assignment clarifications and team-based communication. As such, we highly recommend that students install Slack on their phones / desktop with notifications enabled.

The course staff will also hold weekly office hours to provide support with course materials, assignments, and the project. You can find the office hours schedule here on the course website.

You can contact the course staff via both Slack and email. When contacting the course staff, please message the instructor and the teaching assistants at the same time.

docs.title: Teamwork
docs.text:
Teamwork is an essential part of this course. The extended project is done in teams of 3-5 students. Teams will be assigned by the instructors and stay together for the entire project. Project milestones have a component that is graded for the entire team and a component that is graded individually.

You already have experience working in software teams from 17-313; in this course, teams must coordinate around a live production system that keeps running for several weeks. We expect significant efforts in attempting to address team issues before asking the instructor and teaching assistants to step in. However, we will always be available to provide advice on how to navigate these issues.

docs.title: Textbook
docs.text: Various readings throughout the semester are available online or through the library. Many readings come from the (freely available) book Machine Learning in Production: From Models to Products by Christian Kästner, which accompanies the course this class is adapted from. Additional readings are assembled from different sources and linked from the schedule.

docs.title: Devices in Lecture, Labs, and Recitation
docs.text: Research shows that using devices on non-class related activities harms both the device user's learning, and other students' learning as well. Therefore, in general, we do not allow the use of laptops during lecture. Occasionally we will do activities that require a laptop, but we will make it clear when those are going to take place. We do allow tablets with stylus use if they are flat on the desk and are being used as "digital paper" notetaking. Note that labs and recitations are hands-on and require devices, so please do bring your laptop!

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Evaluation will be based on the following proposed distribution: 35% individual assignments, 30% team project, 20% midterms, 10% labs, 5% participation. There is no final exam.

docs.title: Assignments, Project, Labs, and Exams
docs.text:
The detailed list and due dates are on the schedule; everything below is tentative.

  • Individual assignments (35%). A small number of individual assignments combine implementation, evaluation, and written analysis applying course concepts, for example building and evaluating a recommendation model, analyzing risks and planning for mistakes, and evaluating the security of an AI agent.
  • Team project (30%). In teams, you build, deploy, evaluate, and maintain a movie recommendation service serving a workload of one million active users, through a sequence of milestones (M1-M4) that cover infrastructure, deployment, monitoring and continuous delivery, and an operations agent. Your service runs for several weeks and is assessed on how it holds up under load and changing conditions, as well as on the quality of your engineering decisions and evaluation.
  • Labs (10%). Hands-on sessions with production AI engineering tools and workflows (for example stream processing, model testing, continuous integration, monitoring, and agent tooling). Labs are designed to be completed during the session and directly support the project.
  • Midterms (20%). Two midterms assess your ability to apply course concepts and reason through engineering decisions and tradeoffs.

Assignments are designed to be done by you. Large Language Models can produce plausible-looking answers to many of the questions, but outsourcing this work completely bypasses the cognitive friction required to actually learn the material, and the midterms will test exactly the reasoning the assignments practice. Working through the problems yourself, making mistakes early, and resolving questions in office hours is the best path to success.

docs.title: Regrades
docs.text: Regrade requests can be submitted via Gradescope. The regrade period is open for one week after grades have been released for a particular assignment. After the regrade window is closed, we will not revisit grade assignments.

docs.title: Final Grades
docs.text:
Final grades in this course strictly follow standard mathematical rounding (e.g., 89.5% rounds up to 90.0%, while 89.4% does not). If you believe there was a legitimate mathematical or recording error in your overall grade calculation, please reach out and we will gladly fix it. Beyond verified computational errors, final grades are strictly non-negotiable.

To maintain complete fairness across the entire class, we do not entertain post-semester grade appeals, offer individual extra credit, or grant makeup work to alter final outcomes. Requests to bump a grade by a point or two will be denied. Furthermore, late inquiries regarding past assessments, such as disputing early participation scores or requesting regrades long after an assignment's dedicated window has closed, will not be considered. All regrade requests must be submitted during the designated regrade period for each specific assignment during the term. We will not reopen past grades or adjust individual grade boundaries after the semester has ended.

docs.title: Participation
docs.text:
Participation points in this class are earned through pre-lecture reading assignments, lecture activities, and recitations. To accommodate for life's uncertainties (e.g. health issues, scheduling conflicts), you will automatically get full points for up to four missed participation activities to account for any absences. You do not need to email instructors individually for one-off absences of this sort.

There will be no make-ups for participation points, but you are strongly encouraged to come to office hours to learn or review the materials that you may have missed.

If you find yourself in a situation that calls for an extended absence, please have your academic advisor reach out to the instructors, and they will work to find a solution on a case by case basis.

docs.title: Assignments and Project
docs.text: Late work will receive feedback but no credit. Due to heavy emphasis on planning & teamwork in this course there are no late days; we expect that you anticipate unexpected events in your planning, and coordinate with your teammates when they arise. Exceptions to this policy will be made only in extraordinary circumstances, almost always involving a family or medical emergency, with your academic advisor or the Dean of Student Affairs requesting the exception on your behalf.

docs.title: Time Management
docs.text: This is a 9-unit course, and it is our intention to manage it so that you spend close to 9 hours a week on the course, on average. In general, about 3 hours/week will be spent in lectures, labs & recitations and 6 hours on readings, assignments, and the project. Notice that the project is done in teams and your service runs live for several weeks, so please account for the overhead and decreased time flexibility that comes with team work and operating a production system. Throughout the semester, please feel free to give the course staff feedback on how much time the course is taking for you.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text: Describing tradeoffs among decisions and communication with less technical stakeholders are key aspects of this class. Most assignments and project milestones have a component that requires discussing issues in written form or reflecting about experiences. To practice writing skills, the Academic Resource Center (ARC) offers individually-tailored English language support for students, along with workshops. The instructors are also happy to provide additional guidance if requested.

docs.title: Policy on use of Generative AI for Coding
docs.text: You may use generative AI for any and all coding tasks in the course. However, as we discuss in class, we believe that there are significant implications for your own learning around your AI usage patterns. Our goal for you in this class is that you learn to use AI in a way that helps you become a better engineer, and, since this course is about building AI-powered systems, that you think critically about the AI tools you use as well as the ones you build.

docs.title: Policy on use of Generative AI for Writing
docs.text: You may use generative AI technologies such as Gemini or Claude for assisting in code development. We Very Strongly Discourage using AI to Generate writing responses, but we encourage its use for editing your writing. In addition you are liable for factually inaccurate answers or unspecific rambling produced by AI tools, and we will assess significant penalties to low quality (AI Slop) responses. It is your responsibility to validate and verify AI-produced content before submitting it for class purposes.

docs.title: Professionalism
docs.text:
Your classmates are your colleagues. This is particularly true in this course, where we aim to provide you with principles, practices, tools, and paradigms that will enable you to be an effective, real-world engineer of AI-powered systems. We ask that you treat one another like the professionals you are and that you are preparing to be.

To that end, we will not tolerate harassment in this class. We define harassment as unwelcome or hostile behavior of an ad hominem nature, i.e., that focuses not on ideas but on people and identity. This includes offensive verbal or written comments in reference to gender, sexual orientation, disability, physical appearance, race, or religion; sexual images in public spaces; deliberate intimidation, stalking, following, harassing photography or recording, sustained disruption of class meetings, inappropriate physical contact, and unwelcome sexual attention.

Harassment is against the law and we have no tolerance for it, and neither does the university. Even when behavior does not rise to the level of harassment (even if you think you're "just joking!"), it can still make people very uncomfortable, and harm their educational and professional career by forcing them to devote mental energy to something other than the material they are trying to learn or the professional successes they are trying to achieve. However, we expect that we do not need to threaten you to earn your respect on this matter: we simply ask that you treat one another like professionals, in the most positive sense.

This has two implications:

  • If you feel someone is violating these principles (for example, with a joke that could be interpreted as sexist, racist, or exclusionary), and you feel you have the standing to do so, speak up! Do not be a bystander to unprofessional behavior.
  • If you do not feel comfortable doing so, and/or if the behavior persists, send a private email to the course instructors or set up a meeting with us to discuss the matter. We will preserve your anonymity. We, the course staff, are committed to affording you the same respect we ask you to afford one another. If you feel that we are not doing so, we hope you will feel comfortable either telling us so directly, or approaching another one of the course staff with your concerns.

(Thank you to Shriram Krishnamurthi and Evan Peck for sharing their own policies, from which we drew inspiration for this one.)

docs.title: Academic Honesty and Collaboration
docs.text:
The usual policies apply, especially the University Policy on Academic Integrity. The project is done in teams. We expect that team members collaborate with one another, but that teams work independently from one another, not exchanging results with other teams. Within teams, we expect that you are honest about your contribution to the team's work. This implies not taking credit for others' work and not covering for team members that have not contributed to the team. Otherwise, our expectations regarding academic honesty and collaboration for team work are the same as for individual work.

In-class participation, lab, and recitation activities explicitly require that you are in class to participate. If you are not present, but still submit a participation (e.g., if someone sends you a link), then that is treated as an academic integrity violation. Remote participation activities (such as the teamwork survey) are not covered by this.

The course includes both individual assignments and individual components of team project milestones. Although your solutions for individual parts will be based on the content produced for the team component (e.g. written reflections on lessons learned), we treat individual components of team milestones as equivalent to individual assignments overall, and expect you to complete such components independently of your teammates.

The rest of this academic honesty and collaboration content is taken from the policy used in 17-214:

"You may not copy any part of a solution to a problem that was written by another student, or was developed together with another student, or was copied from another unauthorized source such as the Internet. You may not look at another student's solution, even if you have completed your own, nor may you knowingly give your solution to another student or leave your solution where another student can see it.

Here are some examples of behavior that are inappropriate:

  • Copying or retyping, or referring to, files or parts of files (such as source code, written text, or unit tests) from another person or source (whether in final or draft form, regardless of the permissions set on the associated files) while producing your own. This is true even if your version includes minor modifications such as style or variable name changes or minor logic modifications.
  • Getting help that you do not fully understand, and from someone whom you do not acknowledge on your solution.
  • Writing, using, or submitting a program that attempts to alter or erase grading information or otherwise compromise security of course resources.
  • Lying to course staff.
  • Giving copies of work to others, or allowing someone else to copy or refer to your code or written assignment to produce their own, either in draft or final form. This includes making your work publicly available in a way that other students (current or future) can access your solutions, even if others' access is accidental or incidental to your goals. Beware the privacy settings on your open source accounts!
  • Coaching others step-by-step without them understanding your help.

If any of your work contains any statement that was not written by you, you must put it in quotes and cite the source. If you are paraphrasing an idea you read elsewhere, you must acknowledge the source. Using existing material without proper citation is plagiarism, a form of cheating. If there is any question about whether the material is permitted, you must get permission in advance. We will be using automated systems to detect software plagiarism.

It is not considered cheating to clarify vague points in the assignments, lectures, lecture notes; to give help or receive help in using the computer systems, compilers, debuggers, profilers, or other facilities; or to discuss ideas at a very high level, without referring to or producing code.

Any violation of this policy is cheating. The minimum penalty for cheating (including plagiarism) will be a zero grade for the whole assignment. Cheating incidents will also be reported through University channels, with possible additional disciplinary action (see the above-linked University Policy on Academic Integrity).

If you have any question about how this policy applies in a particular situation, ask the instructors or TAs for clarification."

Note that the instructors respect honesty in these (and indeed most!) situations.

docs.title: Accommodations
docs.text:
Carnegie Mellon University is committed to providing reasonable accommodations for all persons with disabilities. To access accommodation services you are expected to initiate the request and submit a Voluntary Disclosure of Disability Form to the office of Health & Wellness or CaPS-Q. In order to receive services/accommodations, verification of a disability is required as recommended in writing by a doctor, licensed psychologist or psycho-educational specialist. The office of Health & Wellness, CaPS-Q and Office of Disability Resources in Pittsburgh will review the information you provide. All information will be considered confidential and only released to appropriate persons on a need to know basis.

Once the accommodations have been approved, you will be issued a Summary of Accommodations Memorandum documenting the disability and describing the accommodation. You are responsible for providing the Memorandum to your professors at the beginning of each semester.

For more information on policies and procedures, please visit Assistance for Individuals with Disabilities on Scotty.

docs.title: Policy on Healthcare-Related Absence
docs.text: We don't record our lectures, because they are highly interactive and tricky to record, but we do post slides at the end of the day. Please go over them and come to any of the instructors' office hours to discuss the material.

docs.title: A Note on Self Care
docs.text:
We all feel stress at different times and for different reasons, and when we do, it is good to reach out for support. Do your best to maintain a healthy lifestyle by eating well, exercising, getting enough sleep and taking some time to relax. Please know that you are not alone. There are many helpful resources available on campus and an important part of the college experience is learning how to ask for help. Asking for support sooner, rather than later, can often help your situation from getting more complicated. If you or any of your CMUQ peers are experiencing academic stress, difficult life events, or feelings like anxiety or depression, we strongly encourage you to seek support.

Our Student Affairs staff are here to help:

  • Dr. Dalia Rehal, Associate Dean for Student Affairs (CMB 1094), drehal@qatar.cmu.edu, 4454-8545
  • Amie Rollins, Office of Health and Wellness (CMB 1103), amier@andrew.cmu.edu, 4454-8680
  • Dr. Atorina Benjamin, Counseling and Psychological Services (CMB 1104), atorinab@qatar.cmu.edu, 4454-8525

You can also visit the Ilona Wyers Student Lounge and connect with anyone on the Student Affairs Team. Consider also reaching out to a friend, faculty, staff, or family member you trust for help. If you would like to speak to a trained professional for mental health support, day or night, call our ProtoCall hotline at 5554 7913, which is staffed by trained mental health care providers.

If the situation is life threatening, call 999.
